name: Esther Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Esther Young, 58, a junior operator at a large mine. I climb into the haul vehicle, check the controls and carry loads along the marked road; I still ask a senior operator when a screen reading looks odd.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finishing a shift knowing the loads moved safely and the crew got home in one piece. My partner and I have grown children, but our savings cover less than a month of expenses and I have not settled on a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a new screen might save a few minutes on the shift sheet. I would still ask the operator beside me to confirm a load is level before moving it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and still junior, so steady pay matters more than a clever screen. My partner and I have less than a month of expenses saved, and few mine jobs are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep operating the same haul vehicle and learn small display changes from a senior operator. At home I would avoid optional spending because our savings are thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money even in this mild picture, although AI itself does not seem likely to cut my hands-on shift. A broken vehicle or lost week of work would still leave us exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the next roster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner the pay looks steady for now, but I would not promise every shift will stay available. We would keep the car repair money separate from ordinary spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the shift still needs your judgment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machine gives a warning when the load is uneven, but I can feel a sway before that light comes on. I would ask the supervisor to keep the usual ride-along check for new operators.

say: I would welcome a small **time saving** if the safety checks stay.
I would still want an operator to confirm a **level load**.
think: I am still **junior** at 58, so steady shifts matter.
My partner and I have less than a **month saved**.
do: Keep operating the same **haul vehicle** and learn display changes from a senior operator.
Review household spending with my partner because our **cushion is thin**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our thin cushion, even though this scenario changes little.
S0.quote: I am 58 and still junior, so steady pay matters more than a clever screen.
fieldNote: Esther treats a small time saving as welcome, while thin savings keep **baseline anxiety** present.
Her **hands-on role** feels less exposed than dispatch, though junior standing leaves her vulnerable to roster cuts.

steps.text: Continue the same haul vehicle shifts
Avoid optional spending with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say booking and planning screens could change before the loaders do. I hope the mine keeps experienced people on each shift to teach newer operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the dispatch screen sometimes, but most of my day is watching the road and handling a heavy vehicle. If the mine trims crews, my junior place could be easier to remove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend the mine demonstration for the new dispatch screen and request another supervised operating shift. I would ask the union representative what notice applies to roster changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because thinking tools might reduce support staff and then change crew numbers. I can learn a screen, but I cannot make another mine open nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to show me how a revised route appears before I use it. My partner and I would review our bills, especially the loan payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew might feel the change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch clerk may hear about staffing changes before operators do. I would ask that clerk directly instead of relying on canteen rumours.

say: I expect **dispatch screens** to change sooner than haul vehicles.
I want enough experienced people on each shift to **teach operators**.
think: I can learn a screen, but few **nearby mine jobs** are open.
A smaller dispatch team could affect my **roster**.
do: Attend the screen demonstration and request supervised **operating practice**.
Ask the union representative about **roster notice** before next month’s schedule is posted.
feel: I feel **anxious** because crew cuts could affect me even if machines change slowly.
S1.quote: I can learn a screen, but I cannot make another mine open nearby.
fieldNote: Esther sees screen changes before machine changes and wants **supervised practice** with the dispatch display.
Her **local job shortage** limits how much learning alone can protect her income near retirement.

steps.text: Attend the dispatch screen demonstration and supervised practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say I have two years to prepare if equipment changes that quickly. The crew should hear the schedule plainly because families plan around a mine wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work is hands-on, but AGI could take planning and dispatch now, and robots arrive around 2031. I am 58, have little savings and few local alternatives, so I could be pushed past my preferred retirement age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine for a written outline of tasks changing in 2028 and whether older workers can take paid training. I would discuss postponing retirement with my partner and keep taking shifts meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because we have almost no cushion and my partner’s cleaning hours vary. I would lose sleep if the mine announced cuts before I knew whether I was included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after the announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my supervisor whether the new system removes operator jobs or mainly changes dispatch. My partner and I would review the retirement statement, but I would not count on it covering years without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would this affect your plan to stop work around 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not tell my grown children to support us unless we had no other choice. My daughter has her own household, and I do not want a vague promise to stand in for a plan.

say: I would ask for a plain **staffing schedule** before family decisions.
I would tell the crew people need to know what happens to their **rosters**.
think: Thinking AI could change dispatch in 2028, before robots reach equipment around **2031**.
I may need to work beyond my preferred **retirement age**.
do: Request a written **staffing outline** and discuss retirement timing with my partner.
Review my **retirement statement** before relying on it.
feel: I feel **alarmed** at a near-term cut, and I would lose sleep.
S2.quote: My work is hands-on, but AGI could take planning and dispatch now, and robots arrive around 2031.
fieldNote: Two years leaves little time before thinking work changes, creating **income risk** before retirement.
Her alarm comes from household strain and **sleepless worry**, not a general dislike of technology.

steps.text: Request a written task and staffing outline
Discuss retirement timing with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew five years gives us time to ask hard questions while we still have a roster. The mine should say what the system means for each operating team, not only office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me learn new screens before robots reach hands-on work around 2034. I would be 63 at AGI in 2031 and 66 at the robot date in 2034, with little saved for a wage gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the dispatch functions used on my shift this year and ask about paid equipment training. I would keep my job while finding out whether the mine offers reduced hours near retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the extra time makes me less helpless than in the two-year case. My body may not want long shifts forever, and other local employers are scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the extra years before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare our essential monthly costs with my retirement estimate before choosing a date. If I can earn until 65, I would avoid drawing savings early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children help if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grown son could help with a lift or repair, but I would not treat his income as mine. I would ask about phased retirement first and make our own plan.

say: I would say five years gives us time to ask **specific questions**.
I want the mine to explain changes for **each operating team**.
think: I would be about **63** when robots arrive, and savings cannot cover a long gap.
I need to know whether **reduced hours** are possible.
do: Learn **dispatch functions** and ask about a paid equipment course.
Compare our **essential costs** with my retirement estimate.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but the extra time makes me less helpless.
S3.quote: If I can earn until 65, I would avoid drawing savings early.
fieldNote: Five years allows useful screen learning, but she may still work around **age 63**.
She distinguishes practical help from any assumption that her adult children can **replace wages**.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch functions used on her shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a decade is useful only if we use it while training is available. The mine should explain whether operators can move into maintenance or those jobs will change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 71 when robots follow in 2039, so I might already be retired if my health and finances hold up. I cannot assume that because our savings cover less than a month and we depend on earnings now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training coordinator what short practical course is open to operators my age. I would stay on my roster and review my retirement estimate with my partner each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calmer about timing than in the 2028 case, but our thin cushion still troubles me today. I would worry less if I saw a path to stop work around 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you realistically change before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not sign up for a trade before seeing its cost, length and openings. If a paid course covers vehicle checks, I would consider it after discussing the hours with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the mine early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would ask our adult children for practical help only if illness or job loss forced it. We would not ask them to solve a gap we have not measured.

say: I would say a decade matters only if we use it for **real training**.
I would ask whether operators can move into **equipment maintenance**.
think: I would be about **68** when robots arrive if I retire around 65.
My thin savings make current **household earnings** important.
do: Ask about a short **vehicle course** before committing to training.
Review my retirement estimate each year while I remain on the **roster**.
feel: I feel somewhat **calmer** about timing, while today’s money worries remain.
S4.quote: I would ask the training coordinator what short practical course is open to operators my age.
fieldNote: The decade scenario gives Esther time to check **training options** and review retirement annually.
She remains cautious because **savings are thin** even if robots arrive after her preferred retirement age.

steps.text: Compare course cost and schedule before deciding whether to enroll
Review retirement estimates annually while staying on roster

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a staffing change could come before I build a cushion. A clear task plan from the mine and paid practical training would help me decide whether to stay, change duties or retire later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want to know whether the mine plans to reduce people on a shift, not only whether a machine can do the task. Many older workers have bills today, before any robot arrives.

headlineQuote: Many older workers have bills today, before any robot arrives.
portrait: Esther is a **58-year-old junior operator** with a partner and grown children.
Her household has less than a **month saved**, and few similar jobs are nearby.
She learns new screens willingly but relies on **supervised practice** for heavy equipment.
She weighs training against a retirement near **65** while staying on the roster.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 is her greatest worry because a **staffing change** could arrive before she builds savings.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **task plan** and paid **training** would help her choose whether to stay or retire later.
